sources.entry: Unlocking the Power of JSON Patch

summary.title: Unlocking the Power of JSON Patch
summary.one_liner: JSON Patch (RFC 6902) lets you describe partial updates to a JSON document as a list of operations, using JSON Pointer paths, so clients send only the changes over HTTP PATCH.
keywords: json patch vs json merge patch
json patch operations add remove replace move copy test
takeaways: JSON Patch is a standardized (RFC 6902) format for partial updates, sent over HTTP PATCH, made of atomic operations with op and path fields.
JSON Pointer (slash-separated tokens, with ~0 and ~1 escapes and - for array end) identifies the target location in the document.
The six operations are add, remove, replace, move, copy, and test; a failed test makes the whole patch unsuccessful.
Strengths include precision, efficiency, batching, and validation; weaknesses include complexity, debugging difficulty, object order issues, and security risks from bad move/remove operations.

Libraries such as fast-json-patch (JavaScript), python-json-patch (Python), and JsonPatch for .NET can generate and apply patches; request bodies can be validated with AJV and JSON Schema or at an API gateway.
summary.summary: The article explains JSON Patch as defined in RFC 6902: what problem it solves over HTTP PATCH, how operations and JSON Pointer paths work, and the six operations (add, remove, replace, move, copy, test) with examples. It then lists strengths and weaknesses, such as efficiency versus debugging difficulty, and points to libraries (fast-json-patch, python-json-patch, .NET JsonPatch) and the jsonpatch.me tool. The final sections show generating a patch client-side in TypeScript, applying PATCH requests in Node.js with Express, and validating patch bodies three ways (AJV with JSON Schema, Zuplo gateway with OpenAPI, and fast-json-patch itself). It is a vendor blog post, and it briefly mentions JSON Merge Patch as an alternative.
